title: Industrial in-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen

concept.text: The innovation is to convert kerogen—the organic material in oil-shale rock—into producible oil and gas while the rock remains underground, at a scale and duration suitable for an industrial operation. Heating causes the conversion. The intended capability combines subsurface heating, collection of the resulting fluids, measured positive usable-energy return and effective groundwater protection. A small conversion experiment demonstrates part of this capability; the full innovation requires these functions to work together over a commercial volume.

Shell’s In-situ Conversion Process at Mahogany provides a historical example of the approach. Shell reported small-scale production from heated oil shale and separately investigated groundwater exclusion using a freeze wall. PET-04 concerns the proposed industrial capability beyond that demonstration. Its scope excludes surface retorting, in which rock is excavated for conversion elsewhere, and does not assume that a successful heating experiment establishes commercial operation.

significance.text: The potential resource is exceptionally large. USGS Fact Sheet 2012–3145, published in January 2013, reports 4.285 trillion barrels of oil in place across the three principal Green River Formation basins in Colorado, Utah and Wyoming. Its grade-filtered totals include 1.146 trillion barrels in rock yielding at least 15 gallons per ton and 353 billion barrels at a cutoff of 25 gallons per ton. These are nested resource estimates at different grade thresholds, not quantities to add together and not demonstrated economically recoverable reserves.

Successful industrial conversion could make some of that kerogen resource producible without excavating the converted rock. The direct advance would be an integrated way to manufacture and recover hydrocarbon fluids underground from a solid organic resource. The scale of the in-place resource makes even a limited recoverable fraction potentially consequential, but neither its size nor its grade establishes achievable production rates, energy performance or an eventual industry’s size.

The distinction between resource abundance and usable supply is central. In 2011, USGS explained that it had not estimated economically recoverable oil because an economic recovery method had not yet been developed for Green River Formation oil shale. That statement describes conditions at publication. It supports the historical importance of the recovery problem but cannot establish its status in November 2026.

Conditional synthesis: if the technical milestone were achieved and subsequent economics were favorable, it could support additional petroleum supply and development of some kerogen-rich deposits. Positive net usable-energy return would still leave questions about capital cost, operating cost, water requirements, environmental effects and competitiveness. Avoiding excavation of the converted volume would not by itself establish a low-impact operation or widespread deployability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is sustained conversion and recovery across a pre-defined commercial module, with positive measured net usable-energy return and effective fluid containment under the applicable permit. Shell’s January 2013 account explicitly distinguished small-scale technical success from the commercial proof still sought. The supplied historical evidence does not establish whether this integrated capability remains unavailable in November 2026.

Engineering synthesis: the scale-up problem is to deliver enough heat throughout the intended rock volume, sustain conversion, and recover the resulting fluids at a useful rate while controlling their movement. These functions must remain coordinated over years, including the operation of heating, pumping, processing and containment systems. Laboratory pyrolysis alone cannot establish field-scale heat delivery, fluid recovery or containment performance.

Groundwater control is a distinct engineering barrier. Shell investigated a freeze wall to exclude groundwater from the conversion area, showing that isolation was a separate development task alongside conversion. The supplied review does not establish complete containment performance across an industrial operation. It also provides no measured energy balance with which to determine whether heating, containment and production together yielded more usable energy than they consumed.

The earlier description of closely spaced electric production heaters, conduction-dominated heating, quantified slowness and high electricity demand is not established by the supplied evidence. The spacing identified in the review concerns freeze holes, not production heaters. Heat delivery and energy demand remain essential matters to measure, but this record cannot assign a production-heater geometry, heating timescale or energy penalty.

current_state.text: Shell’s Mahogany technology page, archived on 23 January 2013, reports that the Mahogany Demonstration Project South recovered 1,700 barrels of light oil plus associated gas from a 30-by-40-foot testing area. Shell characterized the process as technically successful at small scale, with commercial proof remaining. The reported oil volume is a cumulative recovery figure; the supplied account does not provide the production duration or complete energy accounting needed to infer a sustained industrial production rate or net energy return. No gas quantity is supplied here.

On 25 September 2013, Bill Lehane’s Upstream article reported Shell’s decision to end its Colorado Mahogany oil-shale research project after more than 15 years. The retained article opening supports that dated announcement. The supplied review found that the article text ends mid-sentence despite the extraction metadata indicating no truncation, so the available excerpt cannot support a fuller account of the decision or subsequent industry history.

The supplied evidence establishes historical small-scale conversion and an announced research-project termination. It contains no auditable bounded search results establishing subsequent Green River commercialization or the state of field methods as of November 2026. Consequently, neither the assertion that no in-situ industry followed nor a present-day pilot-scale ceiling can be concluded from this record. This evidence gap does not invalidate Shell’s dated demonstration or prove that later industrial success did or did not occur.

The resource and development evidence also have different access boundaries. According to the supplied review, the complete extracted text and table of the January 2013 USGS resource fact sheet support its numerical estimates; its figures were not inspected. The 2011 economic-method statement was available in a publication abstract, rather than the full four-page report. Shell’s retained webpage text appeared complete, but its referenced research chart was not supplied or inspected. These limitations constrain additional conclusions beyond the specific findings reported here.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: define a commercial module before testing, including its rock volume, relevant geological conditions, conversion-temperature target, operating duration and minimum production rate. Demonstrate conversion and production for years at the declared rate, with operating interruptions and recovery totals reported. The supplied record does not justify numerical thresholds for module size, temperature, duration or rate. Shell’s 30-by-40-foot demonstration would not satisfy the proposed industrial-scale criterion by itself.
completion_criteria.label: Commercial module sustains declared production rate for years

completion_criteria.text: Proposed energy test: measure the usable energy in recovered products and all material energy inputs over a declared accounting boundary and period. Include heating, containment, pumping and processing, and disclose how construction, startup, shutdown and externally supplied utilities are treated. Demonstrate positive net usable-energy return with uncertainty reported. A result based only on heater input or gross oil output would leave the integrated energy requirement unresolved.
completion_criteria.label: Positive net usable-energy return accounts for all material energy inputs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed containment test: verify groundwater performance against the host regulator’s permit and independently assess fluid movement around the conversion volume. Declare monitoring locations, relevant substances, detection limits, baseline conditions and the observation period, including an appropriate period after heating and production end. Permit compliance would be necessary under this proposal, but would not alone establish comprehensive containment beyond the permit’s measured scope.
completion_criteria.label: Groundwater permit compliance and independently assessed subsurface fluid movement

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: make the operating methods, production records, energy accounting and environmental measurements available for independent assessment, and repeat the result in additional modules or relevant geological settings. Such demonstrations would establish performance across the tested conditions, not universal applicability to oil shale. Meeting the technical criteria would still require a separate assessment of profitability and practical deployment constraints.
completion_criteria.label: Independently assessable results reproduced in additional modules or geological settings

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: PET-05, “Shale-oil recovery from the matrix,” shares a focus on obtaining oil from shale-related rock. PET-04 specifically requires conversion of kerogen into fluids underground; PET-05’s title identifies recovery from the matrix as its target. These remain separate capabilities. The supplied record does not provide a detailed PET-05 definition or evidence supporting a broader comparison with tight-oil production.

Roster-based comparison: PET-09, “Bitumen that flows at native reservoir temperature,” targets bitumen mobility, while PET-11, “In-reservoir conversion of bitumen to pipeline-specification crude,” targets conversion to a specified product quality. PET-04 instead targets conversion of kerogen-bearing oil shale at industrial scale. It shares subsurface production challenges with PET-09 and conversion challenges with PET-11, but does not inherit either concept’s feedstock, native-temperature condition or pipeline-quality endpoint. These distinctions follow from the supplied concept titles; no additional comparative performance claims are established.

Roster-based comparison: PET-03, “Commercial gas production from methane hydrate,” likewise concerns making a subsurface resource commercially producible, but addresses a different material and product. PET-06, “Hydrogen from petroleum reservoirs, with the other products left underground,” shares an underground-conversion theme while specifying hydrogen recovery and retention of other products. PET-04 seeks production of oil and gas from kerogen and does not imply the product-retention capability of PET-06.

Roster-based comparison: PET-01, “Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow,” and PET-08, “Permeability and saturation measured through the reservoir volume,” concern prediction and measurement that could help assess fluid recovery and containment in an in-situ conversion project. PET-02, “Conventional-oil recovery at gas-field recovery factors,” concerns recovery of an existing conventional-oil resource. Success in any of these would not alone establish PET-04’s heating, conversion, energy or industrial-operation requirements.

Roster-based comparison: PET-07, “Deep well construction without a steep depth penalty,” could affect the practicality of accessing and instrumenting subsurface operations. PET-10, “A pressure plan with a prospectively tested earthquake bound,” concerns a separate operational risk capability wherever pressure management is relevant. PET-04 does not establish either economical deep-well construction or a tested earthquake bound, and the supplied record does not establish how strongly either capability would constrain a particular conversion project.

Scope distinction: surface retorting is outside PET-04 because its conversion step occurs after excavation. The earlier reference to commercial Estonian kukersite practice is not retained as an established comparison: the supplied evidence does not document that practice. This evidentiary limit does not alter the distinction between surface processing and the in-situ capability defined here.

unresolved_issues: Whether any later Green River project demonstrated sustained industrial in-situ conversion by November 2026 remains unestablished in the supplied record.
The supplied Mahogany evidence does not resolve production duration, associated-gas quantity, complete energy inputs, net usable-energy return or industrial containment performance.

Commercial-module size, conversion temperature, multi-year duration, production targets, energy-accounting conventions and post-operation monitoring periods remain to be specified for a convincing demonstration.
The economically recoverable fraction, commercial competitiveness and practical deployment scale cannot be inferred from the USGS in-place resource estimates.

The original review recommended removing the PET-09/PET-11 comparisons from the evidence-backed significance claim. Their unsupported empirical form was removed, but conceptual distinctions were retained under related_concepts because the supplied roster explicitly identifies the different targets.
The supplied record does not establish commercial Estonian kukersite practice; that factual comparison remains unresolved and is not used to support PET-04.

brief.title: Making oil and gas from rock underground
possible: Oil producers could turn kerogen—the organic material in oil-shale rock—into oil and gas without digging up the rock. They would heat it underground and collect the resulting fuels.
An industrial operation would keep this working for years, recover more usable energy than the whole operation consumes, and protect groundwater.
why: This could add petroleum supply from deposits whose organic material remains locked in solid rock. Producers could develop some of those deposits while leaving the converted rock underground.
The Green River Formation contains an estimated 4.285 trillion barrels of potential oil within its rock. Making even a limited share producible could make a consequential contribution to supply.

sources.showed: The survey estimated that Green River Formation oil shale contains 4.285 trillion barrels of potential oil. It also assessed how much lies in richer rock.
sources.quote:
Using a geology-based assessment methodology, the U.S. Geological Survey estimated a total of 4.285 trillion 
barrels of oil in-place in the oil shale of the three principal basins of the Eocene Green River Formation.
sources.cited_for: The size of the underground resource explains why developing a workable recovery method could matter.
sources.not_established: The assessment does not establish how much oil can be recovered economically.

sources.who: R. C. Johnson, T. J. Mercier and Michael E. Brownfield, USGS
sources.showed: They assessed oil-shale resources in the Greater Green River Basin. At publication, they did not estimate economic recovery because no economic recovery method had been developed.
sources.quote: Green River Formation oil shale also is present in the Piceance Basin of western Colorado and in the Uinta Basin of eastern Utah and western Colorado, and the results of these assessments are published separately.
sources.cited_for: The assessment distinguishes oil present in rock from oil that can be recovered economically.
sources.not_established: It does not establish present-day recovery methods or their economics.

sources.showed: Shell reported recovering 1,700 barrels of light oil plus gas in a small underground heating test. It separately studied a frozen underground barrier to exclude groundwater.
sources.quote: Our research to date has demonstrated that our In situ Conversion Process (ICP) works technically on a small scale - what remains is to prove it can work commercially.
sources.cited_for: Shell demonstrated small-scale underground conversion and treated groundwater isolation as a separate engineering task.
sources.not_established: The test does not establish sustained industrial output, a complete energy balance or industrial groundwater containment.

sources.showed: Lehane reported Shell’s decision to end its Colorado Mahogany research project.
sources.quote: Shell has decided to end its Mahogany oil shale research project in Colorado after more than 15 years and a capital outlay of “many tens of millions of dollars”.
sources.cited_for: Shell ended the research project that had demonstrated small-scale conversion.
sources.not_established: The project’s closure does not establish whether later projects achieved industrial conversion.

shown: Shell reported recovering 1,700 barrels of light oil, plus gas, by heating oil shale underground at Mahogany in Colorado. Shell described this as technical success at small scale, with commercial proof still ahead.
Shell separately investigated groundwater exclusion using a frozen underground wall. It later ended the Mahogany research project.
missing: An industrial operation must sustain useful production across a defined rock volume for years.
A complete energy balance must show that recovered fuels provide more usable energy than the operation consumes.
Groundwater protection and fluid containment must hold during operation and after it ends.
Repeated demonstrations must establish which geological conditions support the combined result.

milestones.label: A commercial unit sustains its declared production rate
milestones.explanation: A defined commercial unit would have to sustain its declared production rate for years, with interruptions and total recovery reported. This would establish that underground conversion can operate at industrial scale.

milestones.label: Recovered fuels deliver a measured energy surplus
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to show an energy surplus after all material inputs, including heating, containment, pumping and processing, with uncertainty stated. This would establish that the whole operation yields usable energy.

milestones.label: Groundwater meets permit limits and fluid movement is assessed
milestones.explanation: Monitoring would have to show groundwater permit compliance, with independent assessment of underground fluid movement during and after operation. This would test containment beyond the substances and locations covered by the permit.

milestones.label: Independently assessable results repeat beyond the initial unit
milestones.explanation: Results would have to be open to independent assessment and repeated in additional units or geological settings. This would establish performance across the tested conditions and help define where the approach works.

uncertain: The commercial unit’s size, production target and operating duration still need convincing definitions.
Energy accounting boundaries and the length of monitoring after operation remain to be specified.
The economically recoverable share, competitiveness and practical scale of deployment remain open questions.

page.title: In-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen
page.definition: An operation heats kerogen—the solid organic matter in oil-shale rock—underground and recovers oil and gas without excavating the converted rock. It completes its permitted commercial production programme with positive net usable-energy output and groundwater within permit limits.

goal.need: BLM reports approximately 4.3 trillion barrels of oil-equivalent resource in place in the Green River Formation. USGS estimates approximately 352 billion barrels in Piceance Basin rock yielding at least 25 gallons per ton. These inventories motivate development of conversion methods; they do not establish economically recoverable reserves.

completion.title: An in-situ oil-shale module meets its production, energy and groundwater tests.
completion.criterion: One module completes the production programme specified in its regulator-approved commercial development plan and meets that plan's output requirements. Usable energy exported as oil and gas exceeds externally supplied energy across construction, heating, containment, pumping, processing and closure. Groundwater meets applicable permit limits during operation and the required post-operation monitoring period. Module dimensions, production quantities and duration are project-specific; no universal numerical values are asserted.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; proposed integrated demonstration test.
completion.basis: BLM oil-shale regulations, the DOE readiness guide and developer demonstration objectives were searched for an integrated industrial production, energy and groundwater test. None was found. BLM lease conversion uses demonstrated production and expected expanded-project economics; its annual production requirements are lease-specific. DOE readiness levels establish system maturity without an oil-shale energy threshold.

milestones.title: An oil-shale conversion system's components work together in laboratory tests.
milestones.criterion: Meet DOE technology readiness level 4: integrated components demonstrate their functions in a laboratory environment. This does not establish underground performance. For oxidative heating, Sun and colleagues reported three repeated fixed-bed experiments using 110–130 kg of oil shale per experiment, published on 6 February 2015. For steam heating, Kang and colleagues' 2021 large-specimen study reported 67.3% overall oil recovery. These results bear on laboratory integration; neither publication supplies a DOE readiness assessment.
milestones.set_by: United States Department of Energy, DOE G 413.3-4A, Table 1, TRL 4; a general maturity criterion, not an oil-shale-specific requirement.

milestones.title: An oil-shale conversion prototype performs its operating functions at engineering or pilot scale.
milestones.criterion: Meet DOE TRL 6: test an engineering-scale prototype capable of all operational functions in an environment closely representing operation. For electrical heating, the assessment dated 29 April 2012 reports 1,860 barrels of oil from one 30-by-40-foot Mahogany South test; this government report is not a peer-reviewed paper. For oxidative heating, Guo and colleagues' 2024 paper reports technical feasibility from Songliao Basin pilot work. Steam heating's cited 2021 result concerns large specimens. These reports do not establish that every TRL 6 function was demonstrated.
milestones.set_by: United States Department of Energy, DOE G 413.3-4A, Table 1, TRL 6; a general maturity criterion, not an oil-shale-specific requirement.

milestones.title: A full-scale oil-shale conversion prototype works in a relevant field environment.
milestones.criterion: Meet DOE TRL 7 by demonstrating the full-scale system prototype in a relevant environment. A component demonstration alone does not meet this system-level test. The 2012 assessment reports that Shell's electrical-heating programme formed a freeze wall across the commercial interval using 136 freeze wells during its 2005–2009 test. Deliberately introduced breaches were detected and resealed. This supports containment-component development, not operation of the complete full-scale conversion system.
milestones.set_by: United States Department of Energy, DOE G 413.3-4A, Table 1, TRL 7; a general maturity criterion, not an oil-shale-specific requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: Full-scale, similar (prototypical) system demonstrated in relevant environment

milestones.title: An in-situ oil-shale project obtains conversion of its BLM research lease to a commercial lease.
milestones.criterion: Obtain BLM approval under 43 CFR 3926.10(c). The project must have produced commercial quantities, paid fair market value, arranged the required socioeconomic mitigation consultation and bonding, and demonstrated that commercial operations can comply with applicable law. Section 3900.2 defines commercial quantities through approved-plan production supporting a reasonable expectation of positive return after production costs and amortized capital costs. This is a United States federal-land authorization test, not proof of industrial operation.
milestones.set_by: Bureau of Land Management, 43 CFR 3900.2 and 3926.10(c); applicable to United States federal oil-shale leases.
milestones.threshold_quote: There have been commercial quantities of shale oil produced from the lease;

milestones.title: The final oil-shale conversion system passes commissioning tests under its expected conditions.
milestones.criterion: Meet DOE TRL 8: the actual system is completed and qualified through testing and demonstration in its final configuration under expected conditions. For an oil-shale operation, the object is the complete conversion and recovery installation, including its selected groundwater-control system. This commissioning result precedes operation over the full production programme required by the completion test.
milestones.set_by: United States Department of Energy, DOE G 413.3-4A, Table 1, TRL 8; a general commissioning criterion, not an oil-shale-specific requirement.

not_found: No outside body was found specifying a combined industrial production, complete energy-balance and groundwater completion test.
No universal module size, production rate or operating duration was found in the BLM oil-shale regulations.
No published DOE readiness assessment was found for the cited oil-shale experiments.
No opened source established completion of the combined test for any listed heating method.
The supplied USGS fact-sheet pages and archived Shell technology page could not be reopened.
The difference between the supplied Shell recovery total of 1,700 barrels and the 2012 assessment's 1,860 barrels was not resolved.

results.finding: One Mahogany South field test recovered 1,700 barrels of oil.
results.detail: Shell reports small-scale oil and gas recovery, but the page does not establish that an engineering-scale prototype demonstrated every operational function required for TRL 6.
results.quote: On only a 30 x 40 foot testing area, Shell successfully recovered 1,700 barrels of high quality light oil plus associated gas from shallower, less-concentrated oil shale layers.

results.finding: Four oil-shale samples were tested in retorts with three different iron powders; the experiments were modeled using electrical heating.
results.detail: The text does not establish that the laboratory retort tests used electrical heating or that integrated electrical-heating components demonstrated their functions. The electrical-heating results described include simulations, not a DOE readiness assessment.
results.quote: The recovery characteristics of four different oil shale samples were tested experimentally using the retort technique. To accomplish efficient temperature distribution, the thermal conductivity of the oil shale samples was increased by the addition of three different iron powders.

results.finding: Steam-injection laboratory test on one 1.34-tonne oil-shale specimen achieved 67.3% overall oil recovery.
results.detail: The laboratory system integrated a steam boiler, a loaded shale specimen, and oil-and-gas condensation and collection. The paper does not provide a DOE readiness assessment or establish underground performance.

results.finding: Oxidative oil-shale pyrolysis was demonstrated in three repeated fixed-bed experiments, each using 110–130 kg of shale.
results.detail: The laboratory system integrated gas supply and heating, a fixed bed, product recovery, and monitoring. The paper does not provide a DOE readiness assessment or establish underground performance.
